body:
You are drafting DIALOGUE TEXT for a video game. Reply in plain text only, in exactly the format asked at the end.

"The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG (think Baldur's Gate 3: fully voiced, branching dialogue, skill checks, a storyteller Narrator). It is folk horror set in Druskenvald, an afterlife realm of endless night under a gargantuan crescent moon with a leering crone's face; an autumn that never ends, pumpkins and bonfires and dead leaves everywhere, but the stakes are real. Humour is deadpan and sits beside the dread. Use only the names given here; invent no new named people, places, monsters or history.

THE PARTY: the player leads four heroes; never name, describe or gender the player's heroes. Some of the party may be these companions, who speak only in the `interject` lines written for them (each line is said only if that companion is present, so it must make sense on its own and never answer another companion's line):
- rook_coldwake: Rook, a Graveborn (undead) fighter, a graveyard rest warden; dry, level, practical, union-minded, cares that the dead are laid to rest properly; few words.
- tobin_hayward: Tobin, a Harvestborn (living scarecrow of wicker and straw) druid; brisk, warm, country-wise, talks about rot, roots, harvests and neighbours; kind under the sharp tongue.
- silas_vane: Silas, a Relicborn (skeleton-folk) monk and card sharp from river landings; fast, cocky, thinks in odds, bets and marks.
- delphine_ravelle: Delphine, a Threadborn (living patchwork doll) warlock; theatrical vaudeville showwoman, says "darling", treats horror as a third-rate sideshow she means to headline.
- lucan_houndstooth: Lucan, a Curseborn (wolf-man) ranger and monster hunter; hushed and earnest, narrates danger like a nature broadcaster, notices scents and tracks.
- cordelia_skein: Cordelia, a Silkborn (spider-folk) sorcerer; cool, cultivated, clinical, delighted by anything morbid as a subject of study.

RULES FOR THE TEXT
- Spoken lines: 1 to 3 short sentences, about 12 to 30 words, never over 40. Contractions are normal. People talk in their own voice and do not explain the plot to the audience. Accent is word choice and rhythm, never phonetic spelling. Country folk of the Hollow speak with a folksy country drawl in their word choice.
- Interject lines: one sentence, under 20 words.
- Option lines (what the player's party says or does): under 12 words, plain, in the party's voice ("We..." or an imperative).
- Narrator lines (the Vagrant, an old train conductor telling the tale afterwards: warm, folksy, wry, a Southern drawl in word choice such as reckon, ain't, folks, a spell, a piece; drop a final g in at most one line in three): second person, present tense, one or two sentences, only what a hero could perceive, concrete senses (smell, sound, texture, cold), no game words (HP, roll, level, check, DC, save, hit points), never tell the player what to feel, never the word "suddenly", never mention a fiddle, never name the Vagrant.
- No stage directions, asterisks, italics, brackets, placeholders, emoji or em dashes (use commas, periods, colons). Straight quotes only. Do not use the arrow characters -> or => inside the text.
- Content is dark but restrained: no gore, no graphic detail.
- Each brief says what the line must do; keep its facts, write it as the speaker would say it.

THIS SCENE: short meetings on the roads of Wickermoor Hollow in Act I, played while the party travels between places on the map. The party arrived by the Ghostlight Express, a ghost train that carries the dead; tonight a shade sabotaged it and it came down in an oak wood, and its dead passengers are scattered, some lost, some turned grey and hostile by the Shroud (a devouring white mist). The nearest town is Wickermoor Village, a timber-framed village round a square with an oak of carved faces. Most villagers follow the Old Ways and worship the Green Queen (a leafy woman's face on their shrines; once a kindly mother of the wood; something has gone wrong with her that nobody says aloud, and a few whisper about "the crooked one"). The Brightsingers are newer settlers who dress bright, carry lanterns, sing hymns to the sun and are building a church. On the hill above the village stands the Druskenvald Estate, a pretty manor where Lord Phillip and Lady Adela Druskenvald have invited the party to dinner; its windows sometimes light on the wrong floors.

Speakers (besides the Narrator and the companions above):
- road_passenger: a dead woman passenger from the Ghostlight Express, in a travelling coat and hat, a ticket in her hand, see-through at the edges; polite, anxious, from somewhere far away; she does not know she is dead and that the train crashed.
- road_bonfire_keeper: an old Old Ways farmer who tends a bonfire of animal bones where two tracks cross on the moor, to keep the Shroud off the road; friendly, slow, a little too interested in what travellers give the fire.
- joan_murdoch: Joan Murdoch, a Brightsinger missionary, the preacher's wife; beaming, warm, relentlessly hopeful; she walks the hill road with lanterns and hymns.

The meetings (the [[n]] markers in this file are yours; everything else is fixed):

```
# Meetings on Act I's roads (data/random_encounters/wreck_road.json and hill_road.json): each plays on its table's map
# (road_moor_bonfire for the wreck road, road_oakwood for the hill road) once, then the journey goes on. Fun pass lane D.
# Drafted by Gemini (docs/plans/gemini_roads), edited; flags in data/flags/roads.json.

# --- A passenger who missed her stop ---

~ lost_passenger
set road_passenger_met
appear road_passenger
Narrator: [[1]]
road_passenger [afraid]: [[2]]
interject name:tobin_hayward: [[3]]
interject name:delphine_ravelle: [[4]]
* [[5]] -> lp_truth
* [[6]] -> lp_lie
* [Religion DC 12] [[7]] -> lp_rest | lp_fail
* [[8]] -> lp_leave

~ lp_truth
road_passenger [sad]: [[9]]
Narrator: [[10]]
inspiration
approve rook_coldwake +2 tobin_hayward +1: You told a lost passenger the truth about the train
-> END

~ lp_lie
road_passenger [smile]: [[11]]
Narrator: [[12]]
interject name:rook_coldwake: [[13]]
approve delphine_ravelle +1 silas_vane +1 rook_coldwake -1: You told a dead passenger her stop was just ahead
-> END

~ lp_rest
Narrator: [[14]]
road_passenger [smile]: [[15]]
Narrator: [[16]]
bless party 2h
approve rook_coldwake +2 tobin_hayward +1: You sent a lost passenger on her way
-> END

~ lp_fail
road_passenger [angry]: [[17]]
Narrator: [[18]]
damage 1d4 psychic party
-> END

~ lp_leave
road_passenger [afraid]: [[19]]
Narrator: [[20]]
-> END

# --- The bone bonfire at the crossing ---

~ bone_bonfire
set road_bonfire_met
appear road_bonfire_keeper at moor_bonfire
Narrator: [[21]]
road_bonfire_keeper [smile]: [[22]]
interject name:lucan_houndstooth: [[23]]
interject name:cordelia_skein: [[24]]
-> bb_menu

~ bb_menu
* [if gold >= 1] [[25]] -> bb_coin
* [[26]] -> bb_hair
* [if not flag.road_bonfire_asked] [[27]] -> bb_ask
* [[28]] -> bb_kick
* [[29]] -> bb_leave

~ bb_ask
set road_bonfire_asked
road_bonfire_keeper: [[30]]
road_bonfire_keeper [sly]: [[31]]
-> bb_menu

~ bb_coin
gold -1
Narrator: [[32]]
road_bonfire_keeper [smile]: [[33]]
temp_hp 1d4+2 party
-> END

~ bb_hair
set road_hair_given
Narrator: [[34]]
road_bonfire_keeper [smile]: [[35]]
Narrator: [[36]]
standing old_ways +1
approve lucan_houndstooth -1 cordelia_skein -1: You gave a lock of hair to a stranger's fire
-> END

~ bb_kick
road_bonfire_keeper [angry]: [[37]]
Narrator: [[38]]
standing old_ways -1
approve silas_vane +1 tobin_hayward -2 rook_coldwake -1: You kicked an old man's bonfire apart
-> END

~ bb_leave
road_bonfire_keeper: [[39]]
-> END

# --- A child on the road ---

~ lost_child
set road_child_met
Narrator: [[40]]
Narrator: [[41]]
interject name:tobin_hayward: [[42]]
interject name:lucan_houndstooth: [[43]]
* [[44]] -> lc_walk
* [Survival DC 12] [[45]] -> lc_point | lc_point_fail
* [[46]] -> lc_leave

~ lc_walk
set road_child_home
time +60
Narrator: [[47]]
Narrator: [[48]]
gold +5
approve tobin_hayward +2 rook_coldwake +1 lucan_houndstooth +1: You walked a lost child home to Wickermoor
-> END

~ lc_point
set road_child_home
Narrator: [[49]]
approve tobin_hayward +1: You showed a lost child the way home
-> END

~ lc_point_fail
set road_child_lost
Narrator: [[50]]
interject name:tobin_hayward: [[51]]
-> END

~ lc_leave
set road_child_lost
Narrator: [[52]]
approve tobin_hayward -2 rook_coldwake -1: You left a child alone on the road
-> END

```

Briefs for the markers:
1. narrator: on the moor road a woman in a travelling coat stands looking up and down the track, ticket in hand; the heather shows through the hem of her coat
2. road_passenger: excuse me, which way is the platform; she cannot miss the Ghostlight, her stop is coming and the conductor promised to call it
3. interject tobin_hayward: quietly, she has the look of somebody still waiting on a harvest that already came in
4. interject delphine_ravelle: darling, nobody has told her the show closed; somebody ought to
5. option: tell her the train came down in the wood
6. option: tell her the next stop is just ahead
7. option: speak the conductor's last call over her, so she can get off
8. option: walk on without a word
9. road_passenger: she looks at her ticket a long while; so that was the jolt; she thanks them for not lying, she had wondered why her hands were cold
10. narrator: she tucks the ticket into the hedge like a bookmark and is not there; the cold she leaves behind smells of coal smoke
11. road_passenger: oh, thank heavens, just ahead; she will tell the conductor they were kind
12. narrator: she sets off briskly along the road and the fog takes her a step at a time; far off a whistle blows that no engine is under
13. interject rook_coldwake: she'll walk that road till it wears through; that's no kindness to the dead
14. narrator: the old words come to the speaker's mouth easy as a hymn; "all stops, end of the line"; she straightens her hat as if she heard a bell
15. road_passenger: so this is mine; she says she has been holding this ticket a very long time
16. narrator: she steps off the road the way folks step off a train, and the fog where she stood warms like a carriage with the stove lit
17. road_passenger: she is not getting off here, this isn't her stop, they cannot make her; her voice goes thin and high
18. narrator: she comes apart into cold mist that goes through every one of you like a January draught, and the road is empty
19. road_passenger: she calls after them, please, which way, she cannot miss it
20. narrator: you hear her asking the empty road for a good while after; then only the wind in the heather
21. narrator: where the two tracks cross, an old man feeds bones to a bonfire; the smoke is greenish and smells of burnt hair and wet leaves
22. road_bonfire_keeper: evening, travellers; the fire keeps the white mist off the crossing; every soul who passes gives it a little something, a coin, a hair, a bone, whatever they can spare
23. interject lucan_houndstooth: hushed, a fire of bones, and an old fellow who sniffs the wind when we come near; curious, very curious
24. interject cordelia_skein: rabbit, sheep, and one that I would rather not name; a fascinating fuel
25. option: drop a coin in the fire
26. option: give the fire a lock of hair
27. option: ask who the fire is for
28. option: kick the bones apart
29. option: warm our hands and go
30. road_bonfire_keeper: for the Green Queen, mother of the wood, who feeds every root and takes back every leaf
31. road_bonfire_keeper: lowering his voice, she has been poorly a long while; the crooked one tends her now, and he is ever so grateful for gifts
32. narrator: the coin goes in with a hiss and the smoke turns from green to gold for a breath; warmth settles into your bones like a second coat
33. road_bonfire_keeper: that'll see you to the next crossing; she remembers a generous traveller
34. narrator: the hair curls and catches, and the old man watches it burn with his whole attention, the way a man reads a letter
35. road_bonfire_keeper: oh, that's a fine gift, a personal one; she will know you now, wherever you go
36. narrator: the smoke leans away from the wind, uphill, toward the dark manor on the rise, and the old man smiles at it
37. road_bonfire_keeper: horrified, not the bones, the mist will have the crossing by morning; he curses them in the old way and scrabbles for the scattered bones
38. narrator: the bones roll smoking into the heather; behind you, the old man's voice keeps calling the Queen's name till it sounds like weeping
39. road_bonfire_keeper: suit yourselves; the fire will be here, and so will he
40. narrator: a small girl in a pumpkin-orange shawl stands in the middle of the road with a basket of mushrooms, staring at you and not saying anything
41. narrator: she points back the way you came toward the far lights of Wickermoor, then at herself, then at the dark woods, and her chin wobbles
42. interject tobin_hayward: some farmer's little one, strayed after mushrooms; somebody's out of their mind looking for her
43. interject lucan_houndstooth: hushed, small footprints, and larger ones following at a distance, then turning back; she is lucky, for now
44. option: walk her home to Wickermoor
45. option: show her the safe way home
46. option: walk on
47. narrator: it's an hour's walk with her small cold hand in yours; at the edge of the village a farm woman runs out of a gate in her nightdress and scoops her up
48. narrator: the woman presses a few coins on you and won't hear no, and the girl looks back over her mother's shoulder at you the whole way in
49. narrator: you show her the line of the road and the lights to keep in front of her; she nods hard, and you watch the orange shawl all the way to the first fence
50. narrator: she listens and nods, then trots off on the wrong fork into the trees, and by the time you call out the shawl is gone
51. interject tobin_hayward: we ought to have walked her; I'll be thinking about that orange shawl a while
52. narrator: you leave her standing in the road; when you look back she is still there, still pointing, and then the fog is there instead

## Reply format
One line per marker, in order, exactly `n => text` (no quotes around the text, no extra lines, no commentary). 52 lines, numbered as above.
